title: Check what is actually running: right code, wrong environment, is the most common wasted hour in software
story:
An engineer edits a file, saves it, and runs the thing. Nothing changes. They add a line that prints an obvious marker, run it again, and the marker does not appear.

What happens next is the waste this lesson is about. They assume the logic is wrong, because the logic is what they were thinking about, and they spend the afternoon rewriting an algorithm that was never executed. The evidence that should have stopped them was available in the first minute: a line they added did not run. That is not a statement about the algorithm. It is a statement about which file the machine is reading.

The causes are boringly various and they all look identical from the inside. The process was started from a different directory than the one being edited. The running container holds an image built yesterday. A build step failed quietly and the artefact being served is the last one that compiled. The browser is serving a cached bundle. A second copy of the process is still listening on the port and answering every request. Something between the editor and the processor is serving a different version of the truth, and nothing in the output says so.

So the discipline is to prove the connection before debugging anything that depends on it. Change something arbitrary and unmistakable — a string nobody would ever write on purpose — and confirm it appears in the output. If it appears, the pipeline from editor to execution is intact and the bug is where you thought. If it does not appear, stop: you do not have a logic problem, you have a delivery problem, and no amount of reasoning about the code will touch it.

The reason this is worth a lesson rather than a footnote is that it inverts the usual order of suspicion. Debugging normally proceeds from the assumption that the code is what is running and the behaviour is wrong. Here the behaviour is telling you the code is not what is running — and that hypothesis is cheap to test and almost never tested first, because it feels like checking whether the computer is plugged in.

problem.name: Verify the execution pipeline
problem.shape: An edit produces no change in behaviour, and the reason may be that the edited code is not the code being executed.
tell: a change has no effect at all, rather than the wrong effect
a line added purely to print something does not print
behaviour matches an older version of the code
the same input behaves differently in two places that should be identical
problem.move: Before reasoning about logic, prove the path from the file you are editing to the thing that runs. Insert an unmistakable marker, confirm it appears, and only then debug. If it does not appear, stop and find where the version diverges rather than continuing to reason about code that is not running.
problem.invariant: A change with no effect whatsoever is evidence about the delivery path, not about the logic. Wrong logic produces wrong behaviour; undelivered code produces unchanged behaviour.
problem.breaks: The marker test proves the path was intact at the moment you ran it, not that it stays intact. A watcher that dies later, a cache that repopulates, or a second process that restarts will put you back where you were — so a passing marker is evidence about one run rather than a property of the setup.

cost.time: seconds, which is why the resistance to doing it is about how the check feels rather than what it costs
cost.beats: reasoning about logic, which cannot distinguish correct code that did not run from incorrect code that did, and restarting everything, which sometimes works and teaches nothing

worked.problem: You change the code and the behaviour does not change at all. What is the first thing to check?
worked.reasoning:
Whether the code you edited is the code that ran — before anything about the logic, because the symptom is already pointing at the delivery path rather than at the algorithm.

The distinction that makes this worth doing first is the shape of the evidence. Wrong logic produces wrong behaviour: something different from what you wanted, which you can reason about. Undelivered code produces unchanged behaviour: exactly what happened before, as though you had done nothing — because, as far as the machine is concerned, you did. Those two symptoms look similar to a person and mean entirely different things.

So the test is to make a change that cannot be confused with anything else. Not a change to the logic, whose absence you might rationalise, but an unmistakable marker printed for no reason — a string nobody would write on purpose. Run it. If the marker appears, the path from your editor to execution is intact, the bug is in the code you were looking at, and you have spent seconds to rule out a whole class of explanation. If it does not appear, you have learned something far more valuable: you do not have a logic problem at all.

The causes then divide quickly and are worth knowing as a list, because they all present identically. The process was started from a different directory than the one being edited. A container is running an image built earlier. A build step failed quietly and the artefact being served is the last one that compiled successfully. A cache is serving an older bundle. A second copy of the process is still bound to the port and answering everything. In each case the code is fine and the delivery is broken, and no amount of reading the source will reveal it.

The reason this is not obvious in the moment is that it inverts the usual order of suspicion. Debugging normally assumes the code is what runs and the behaviour is wrong. This hypothesis says the opposite, and it feels like checking whether the machine is plugged in — which is precisely why people skip it and lose an afternoon to an algorithm that was never executed.

I would add one limitation, because a passing marker can be over-trusted. It proves the path was intact at the moment you ran it. A watcher process that dies later, a cache that repopulates, or a duplicate process that restarts puts you straight back, and the second failure is harder to diagnose because you have already ruled this out once. So the marker is evidence about one run rather than a property of the setup, and when the symptom returns it is worth re-running rather than remembering.

problem.practice: Take the project you are working in now and add a marker that prints something unmistakable at startup. Confirm you see it. Then deliberately break the delivery path — start the process from a different directory, or serve a stale build — and observe that the symptom is identical to a logic bug while being nothing of the kind.

beats.broke: An edit produces no change at all, and the natural reading is that the logic is wrong — so the next hours go to rewriting code that was never executed.
beats.fix: Prove the path from the file you are editing to the thing that runs, by inserting a marker that cannot be mistaken for anything else and confirming it appears before debugging anything that depends on it.
beats.cost: The check takes seconds and feels like checking whether the machine is plugged in, which is why it is skipped — and it proves the path was intact for that run rather than establishing a property of the setup.
